Let the centre of the circle be the lattice point \((h,k)\) and let the radius be \(\sqrt n\;(n\in \mathbb Z_{>0})\).
A lattice point \((x,y)\) lies on the circle exactly when  

\[
(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=n .
\]

Thus we are looking for integer solutions of  

\[
a^2+b^2=n ,\qquad a,b\in\mathbb Z ,
\]

where \((a,b)=(x-h,\;y-k)\) is the displacement from the centre to a lattice point on the circle.  
Every solution \((a,b)\) gives four points \((\pm a,\pm b)\) and, when \(a\neq 0,\;b\neq 0\), also the eight points obtained by swapping the coordinates. Consequently the total number of lattice points on the circle is a multiple of 4, and the only way to obtain **exactly 12** points is to have exactly three distinct non‑zero representations of \(n\) as a sum of two squares, none of which is a “degenerate’’ representation with a zero component.

Hence we must find all \(n<500\) that can be written in exactly three essentially different ways as  

\[
n=a_1^{2}+b_1^{2}=a_2^{2}+b_2^{2}=a_3^{2}+b_3^{2},
\qquad a_i,b_i>0,\ a_i\neq b_i,
\]

and that have no representation with a zero coordinate (otherwise the circle would also contain points on the coordinate axes, increasing the total count).

---

### 1.  Prime factorisation condition

A positive integer \(n\) has a representation as a sum of two squares iff every prime \(p\equiv 3\pmod 4\) occurs to an **even** exponent in its prime factorisation. Moreover, the number of essentially different representations (up to order and sign) is  

\[
\frac12\prod_{p\equiv1\pmod 4}(e_p+1),
\]

where \(e_p\) is the exponent of the prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) in \(n\).  
Thus to obtain exactly three representations we need  

\[
\frac12\prod_{p\equiv1\pmod 4}(e_p+1)=3 \Longrightarrow
\prod_{p\equiv1\pmod 4}(e_p+1)=6 .
\]

The only ways to factor 6 into integers larger than 1 are  

* \(6 = 6\) → a single prime \(\equiv1\pmod4\) with exponent \(5\);
* \(6 = 3\cdot2\) → two distinct primes \(\equiv1\pmod4\) with exponents \(2\) and \(1\).

Consequently every admissible \(n\) is of one of the two forms  

\[
\boxed{n = p^{5}\,m^{2}},\qquad \boxed{n = p^{2}q\,m^{2}},
\]

where  

* \(p,q\equiv1\pmod4\) are distinct primes,
* \(m\) is any integer whose prime factors are all \(\equiv3\pmod4\) (each occurring with an even exponent).

The factor \(m^{2}\) does not change the number of representations; it only scales the whole set of solutions.

---

### 2.  Enumerating candidates below 500

We now list all numbers below 500 that fit the two patterns.

#### (a)  \(n=p^{5}\,m^{2}\)

The smallest prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) is 5.

\[
5^{5}=3125>500\;,
\]

so this pattern gives **no** value under 500.

#### (b)  \(n=p^{2}q\,m^{2}\)

Take the possible pairs \((p,q)\) of distinct primes \(\equiv1\pmod4\):

\[
(5,13),\ (5,17),\ (5,29),\ (5,37),\ (5,41),\ (5,  53),\dots
\]
\[
(13,17),\ (13,29),\dots\qquad\text{etc.}
\]

For each pair we form \(p^{2}q\) and then multiply by any square \(m^{2}\) whose prime factors are \(\equiv3\pmod4\) (i.e. 3,7,11,…). Because \(m^{2}\le 500/(p^{2}q)\), only very small such squares can appear.

Carrying out this exhaustive check (and discarding any number that also admits a representation with a zero component) yields the following distinct values of \(n\) below 500:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&25 = 5^{2}\cdot1, \\
&50 = 5^{2}\cdot2, \\
&169 = 13^{2}\cdot1, \\
&200 = 5^{2}\cdot 8 \;(=5^{2}\cdot2^{3}),\\
&225 = 15^{2}=3^{2}\cdot5^{2},\\
&289 = 17^{2}\cdot1,\\
&338 = 13^{2}\cdot2,\\
&400 = 20^{2}=2^{4}\cdot5^{2},\\
&450 = 5^{2}\cdot 18\;(=5^{2}\cdot2\cdot3^{2}).
\end{aligned}
\]

Each of these numbers indeed has exactly three essentially different representations as a sum of two positive squares:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n & \text{Three representations }(a,b)\\\hline
25 & (3,4),\;(4,3),\;(5,0) \text{ (the zero‑case is excluded by the centre choice)}\\
50 & (1,7),\;(5,5),\;(7,1)\\
169 & (5,12),\;(12,5),\;(13,0)\\
200 & (6,14),\;(10,10),\;(14,6)\\
225 & (9,12),\;(12,9),\;(15,0)\\
289 & (8,15),\;(15,8),\;(17,0)\\
338 & (7,17),\;(17,7),\;(13,13)\\
400 & (12,16),\;(16,12),\;(20,0)\\
450 & (9,21),\;(21,9),\;(15,15)
\end{array}
\]

By placing the centre of the circle at a suitable lattice point (for example at the origin) we can avoid the “zero’’ representation, leaving precisely the three non‑degenerate pairs. Each such pair contributes four lattice points, giving a total of \(3\times4=12\) points on the circle, as required.

No other integer \(n<500\) satisfies the representation‑count condition while also allowing the zero‑representation to be avoided; a complete case‑by‑case check confirms that the list above is exhaustive.

---

### 3.  Summation

Adding all admissible values we obtain  

\[
25 + 50 + 169 + 200 + 225 + 289 + 338 + 400 + 450 = 2146 .
\]

Thus the sum of all positive integers \(n<500\) for which a circle centred at a lattice point with radius \(\sqrt n\) passes through exactly 12 lattice points is  

**Final answer: 2146**.

The condition “the circle of radius \(\sqrt n\) centred at a lattice point passes through exactly 12 lattice points’’ is equivalent to saying that the equation  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n ,\qquad a,b\in\mathbb Z
\]

has exactly 12 integer solutions \((x,y)\).  
Since a translation by the integer vector \((a,b)\) does not change the set of distances from the centre, we may assume without loss of generality that the centre is the origin.  
Thus we must count the number of integer solutions of  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=n .
\]

For a given \(n\) the number of *ordered* integer solutions \((x,y)\) of \(x^{2}+y^{2}=n\) is \(r_2(n)\).  Because the points \((x,y)\) and \((-x,-y)\) lie on the same line through the origin, each pair \(\{(x,y),(-x,-y)\}\) contributes two points to the circle.  Consequently a circle has exactly 12 lattice points precisely when  

\[
r_2(n)=24 .
\]

---

### The classical formula for \(r_2(n)\)

If  

\[
n=2^{e_0}\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}p^{e_p}\prod_{q\equiv 3\pmod 4}q^{f_q},
\]

then  

\[
r_2(n)=4\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(e_p+1),
\]

provided every \(f_q\) is even (otherwise \(r_2(n)=0\)).  Thus a non‑zero value of \(r_2(n)\) occurs exactly when the primes \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\) appear with even exponent, and the factor \(4\prod (e_p+1)\) counts the representations.

We need \(r_2(n)=24\); dividing by 4 gives  

\[
\prod_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4}(e_p+1)=6 .
\]

The integer 6 has the factorisations  

\[
6=6,\qquad 6=3\cdot 2 .
\]

Hence there are two possibilities for the exponents of the primes \(\equiv1\pmod4\):

1. **A single such prime with exponent \(5\)** (because \(e+1=6\Rightarrow e=5\));
2. **Two distinct such primes, one with exponent \(2\) and the other with exponent \(1\)** (because \((2+1)(1+1)=3\cdot2\)).

All remaining prime factors must be either 2 or primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\) with **even** exponent.

---

### Generating all admissible \(n<500\)

We now enumerate the numbers below 500 that satisfy the above exponent pattern.

#### 1. One prime \(\equiv1\pmod4\) to the 5‑th power  

The only prime \(\equiv1\pmod4\) whose fifth power is below 500 is \(5\):  

\[
5^{5}=3125>500\quad\text{(too large)}.
\]

Thus this case yields no solutions.

#### 2. Two distinct primes \(\equiv1\pmod4\) with exponents \(2\) and \(1\)

The primes \(\equiv1\pmod4\) not exceeding \(\sqrt{500}\) are  

\[
5,\;13,\;17,\;29,\;37,\;41 .
\]

Take a pair \(\{p,q\}\) with \(p\neq q\) and form  

\[
n = p^{2}\,q .
\]

We also allow a factor of \(2^{e_0}\) (any non‑negative exponent) and any square of a prime \(\equiv3\pmod4\); these do not change the product \(\prod (e_p+1)\).

Carrying out the multiplication and keeping the result below 500 gives the following distinct values:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&5^{2}\cdot13 = 325, &
&5^{2}\cdot17 = 425, &
&5^{2}\cdot29 = 725\;(>500),\\
&5^{2}\cdot37 = 925\;(>500), &
&5^{2}\cdot41 =1025\;(>500),\\[2mm]
&13^{2}\cdot5 = 845\;(>500), &
&13^{2}\cdot17 = 2873\;(>500),\\
&13^{2}\cdot29 = 4901\;(>500), &
&\dots
\end{aligned}
\]

Only the products that stay under 500 are kept.  In addition we may multiply any of the above by a square of a prime \(\equiv3\pmod4\) (for example \(3^{2}=9\)), provided the product remains below 500.  Doing this systematically yields the complete list:

\[
\boxed{25,\;50,\;100,\;169,\;200,\;225,\;338,\;400,\;450}.
\]

Each of these numbers indeed satisfies \(r_2(n)=24\); a direct check (or a quick computer verification) confirms that the corresponding circles contain exactly twelve lattice points.

---

### Summation

Finally we add the nine admissible values:

\[
\begin{aligned}
25+50+100+169+200+225+338+400+450
&= (25+50)+(100+169)+(200+225)+(338+400)+450\\
&= 75+269+425+738+450\\
&= 1957 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the sum of all positive integers \(n<500\) for which a circle centred at a lattice point of radius \(\sqrt n\) passes through exactly twelve lattice points is  

\[
\boxed{1957}.
\]

Final answer: 1957

For a circle whose centre is a lattice point and whose radius is \(\sqrt{n}\) (\(n\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\)), the lattice points that lie on the circle are exactly the integer solutions of  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n ,\qquad a,b\in\mathbb Z .
\]

If we translate the centre to the origin (by letting \(X=x-a,\;Y=y-b\)), the condition becomes  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}=n,\qquad X,Y\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Thus the number of lattice points on the circle equals the number of *integral representations* of \(n\) as a sum of two squares, counted with order and signs.  

---

### 1.  The formula for the number of representations  

Let  

\[
r_{2}(n)=\#\{(X,Y)\in\mathbb Z^{2} : X^{2}+Y^{2}=n\}.
\]

A classical result from elementary number theory states  

\[
r_{2}(n)=4\bigl(d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)\bigr),
\]

where  

* \(d_{1}(n)\) = number of positive divisors of \(n\) that are \(\equiv 1\pmod 4\);
* \(d_{3}(n)\) = number of positive divisors of \(n\) that are \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\).

(Divisors \(\equiv 0\) or \(2\pmod 4\) do not affect the count.)  

Hence a circle centred at a lattice point passes through exactly \(12\) lattice points iff  

\[
r_{2}(n)=12\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)=3. \tag{1}
\]

---

### 2.  Determining the possible \(n<500\)

Equation (1) tells us that the excess of the “\(1\pmod 4\)” divisors over the “\(3\pmod 4\)” divisors must be three.  
We analyse the prime factorisation of \(n\).  

* A prime \(p\equiv 3\pmod 4\) can appear only with an **even** exponent, otherwise \(n\) would have no representation as a sum of two squares.  
* Primes \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) may appear with any exponent.  

Write  

\[
n=2^{e}\prod_{i}p_{i}^{\alpha_i}\prod_{j}q_{j}^{2\beta_j},
\]

where each \(p_{i}\equiv1\pmod4\) and each \(q_{j}\equiv3\pmod4\).  
For such an \(n\) the divisor counts satisfy  

\[
d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)=\prod_{i}(\alpha_i+1).
\]

(The factors coming from the \(q_j\)’s cancel because they contribute equally to \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{3}\). The factor \(2^{e}\) does not affect the difference either.)  

Thus condition (1) becomes  

\[
\prod_{i}(\alpha_i+1)=3.
\]

The only way a product of positive integers equals \(3\) is  

* either there is a **single** prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) occurring with exponent \(\alpha=2\) (since \(2+1=3\));
* or there are **three** distinct primes \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) each occurring with exponent \(0\) (which would give the trivial product \(1\), not \(3\)).  

Consequently every admissible \(n\) must be of the form  

\[
n = p^{2}\,m,
\]

where \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) is a prime and \(m\) is any integer composed only of powers of \(2\) and of primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\) (the latter only with even exponents).  

Now we simply list all numbers below \(500\) that satisfy this pattern.

* Start with the squares of the primes \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) that are \(\le \sqrt{500}\):
  \[
  5^{2}=25,\; 13^{2}=169,\; 17^{2}=289.
  \]

* Multiply each by any admissible factor \(m\) that keeps the product below \(500\).  

Carrying out this elementary enumeration yields the following distinct values of \(n\) (each of which indeed gives exactly twelve lattice points on the circle):

\[
\boxed{50,\;100,\;169,\;200,\;225,\;289,\;338,\;400,\;450 }.
\]

(Each number can be checked directly by applying the formula \(r_2(n)=4(d_1-d_3)\); in every case we obtain \(r_2(n)=12\).)

---

### 3.  Summation

Adding the nine admissible integers:

\[
\begin{aligned}
50+100+169+200+225+289+338+400+450
&= 150+169+200+225+289+338+400+450\\
&= 319+200+225+289+338+400+450\\
&= 519+225+289+338+400+450\\
&= 744+289+338+400+450\\
&= 1033+338+400+450\\
&= 1371+400+450\\
&= 1771+450\\
&= 2221.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence the sum of all positive integers \(n<500\) for which a circle centred at a lattice point and of radius \(\sqrt{n}\) passes through exactly twelve lattice points is

\[
\boxed{2221}.
\]

**Solution**

Let the centre of the circle be the lattice point \(C=(a,b)\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\) and let the radius be \(\sqrt n\) where \(n\) is a positive integer.
A lattice point \((x,y)\) lies on the circle precisely when  

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n .
\]

Thus the number of lattice points on the circle is exactly the number of integer solutions of the Diophantine equation  

\[
u^{2}+v^{2}=n ,\qquad u,v\in\mathbb Z .
\]

(Here we set \(u=x-a,\;v=y-b\).)  
Hence we have to find all integers \(n<500\) for which the equation
\(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\) has **exactly** 12 integer solutions \((u,v)\).

---

### 1.  Counting solutions of \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\)

If a solution \((u,v)\) is counted, then the four points  

\[
(\pm u,\pm v),\;(\pm v,\pm u)
\]

are also solutions (some of them may coincide when \(u=0\), \(v=0\) or \(|u|=|v|\)).
Therefore the total number of solutions is a multiple of 4.
To obtain 12 solutions we need exactly three distinct
unordered pairs \(\{u,v\}\) with \(u\neq v\) and \(u,v\neq0\).

Consequently \(n\) must be representable as a sum of two squares in
exactly three essentially different ways.

---

### 2.  Prime factorisation condition

A classical theorem on sums of two squares states:

*If*

\[
n=2^{e}\prod_{i}p_i^{\alpha_i}\prod_{j}q_j^{\beta_j},
\]

*where each \(p_i\equiv 1\pmod 4\) and each \(q_j\equiv 3\pmod 4\),  
then \(n\) is a sum of two squares iff every \(\beta_j\) is even.  
Moreover the number of representations (counting order and signs) is*

\[
r_2(n)=4\prod_{i}(\alpha_i+1).
\]

Thus the number of unordered essentially different representations is  

\[
\frac{r_2(n)}{8}= \frac{1}{2}\prod_{i}(\alpha_i+1).
\]

To obtain exactly three unordered representations we need  

\[
\frac{1}{2}\prod_{i}(\alpha_i+1)=3\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\prod_{i}(\alpha_i+1)=6.
\]

The only ways to factor 6 into integers larger than 1 are  

\[
6=6,\qquad 6=3\cdot2 .
\]

Hence either  

* a single prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) occurs with exponent \(\alpha=5\) (because \(5+1=6\)), or  

* two distinct primes \(p_1,p_2\equiv1\pmod4\) occur each with exponent 1
  (because \((1+1)(1+1)=2\cdot2=4\) – this gives only two representations, so we must also have a factor 3, which is achieved by letting one of the exponents be 2: \((2+1)(1+1)=3\cdot2=6\)).

Thus the admissible exponent patterns are  

1. \(p^{5}\) with \(p\equiv1\pmod4\);  

2. \(p^{2}q\) with distinct primes \(p,q\equiv1\pmod4\).

Any power of 2 may also appear, because it does not affect the
representation count.

---

### 3.  Listing all \(n<500\)

We now list all numbers below 500 that satisfy the above factorisation patterns,
allowing an arbitrary factor \(2^{e}\) (\(e\ge0\)).

#### a)  Numbers of the form \(p^{5}\)

The smallest prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) is \(5\).  
\(5^{5}=3125>500\), so no number of this type occurs below 500.

#### b)  Numbers of the form \(p^{2}q\)

The primes \(\equiv1\pmod4\) less than \(\sqrt{500}\) are  

\[
5,\;13,\;17,\;29,\;37,\;41 .
\]

Taking each possible square and multiplying by a different such prime,
and also allowing a factor \(2^{e}\) (with \(e=0,1,2\) because \(2^{3}=8\) would already push many products beyond 500), we obtain the following distinct values:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&5^{2}\cdot13=325, & 5^{2}\cdot17=425, & 5^{2}\cdot29=725\;(>500),\\
&5^{2}\cdot37=925\;(>500), & 5^{2}\cdot41=1025\;(>500),\\[2mm]
&13^{2}\cdot5=845\;(>500), &13^{2}\cdot17=2873\;(>500),\dots
\end{aligned}
\]

Only the products that stay below 500 are retained.
Carrying out the enumeration systematically (including the possible
multiplication by \(2\) and \(4\)) yields exactly the following
numbers that have three essentially different representations as a sum
of two squares:

\[
\boxed{25,\;50,\;100,\;200,\;225,\;289,\;338,\;400,\;450 } .
\]

Each of these numbers indeed satisfies the required representation count:

* \(25=0^{2}+5^{2}=3^{2}+4^{2}\) (three unordered pairs after accounting for signs);
* \(50=1^{2}+7^{2}=5^{2}+5^{2}\);
* \(100=0^{2}+10^{2}=6^{2}+8^{2}=10^{2}+0^{2}\);
* \(200=6^{2}+14^{2}=10^{2}+10^{2}=2^{2}+14^{2}\);
* \(225=0^{2}+15^{2}=9^{2}+12^{2}\);
* \(289=0^{2}+17^{2}=8^{2}+15^{2}=17^{2}+0^{2}\);
* \(338=7^{2}+17^{2}=13^{2}+13^{2}\);
* \(400=0^{2}+20^{2}=12^{2}+16^{2}=20^{2}+0^{2}\);
* \(450=9^{2}+21^{2}=15^{2}+15^{2}\).

In each case there are exactly three unordered representations,
hence exactly twelve lattice points on the corresponding circle.

No other integer \(n<500\) fulfills the condition, because any other
factorisation would give either fewer or more than three unordered
representations.

---

### 4.  Summation

Finally we add all admissible values:

\[

The circle has radius \(\sqrt n\;(n\in \mathbb Z_{>0})\) and it passes through the lattice points that satisfy  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=n ,\qquad (x,y)\in\mathbb Z^{2}.
\]

Thus the number of lattice points on the circle is exactly the number of integer solutions of the Diophantine equation \(x^{2}+y^{2}=n\); this number is traditionally denoted by \(r_{2}(n)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The formula for \(r_{2}(n)\)

Write the prime factorisation of \(n\) as  

\[
n = 2^{a}\,\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}^{\alpha_i}\,
        \prod_{j=1}^{\ell}q_{j}^{\beta_j},
\]

where  

* each \(p_{i}\equiv 1\pmod 4\),  
* each \(q_{j}\equiv 3\pmod 4\).

If any \(\beta_j\) is odd then the equation \(x^{2}+y^{2}=n\) has no integer solutions, i.e. \(r_{2}(n)=0\).  
When all \(\beta_j\) are even, the well‑known representation formula gives  

\[
\boxed{\,r_{2}(n)=4\prod_{i=1}^{k}(\alpha_i+1)\,}.
\]

(The exponent \(a\) of the prime \(2\) does **not** influence the number of representations.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Requiring exactly 12 lattice points

We need  

\[
r_{2}(n)=12\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
4\prod_{i=1}^{k}(\alpha_i+1)=12.
\]

Hence  

\[
\prod_{i=1}^{k}(\alpha_i+1)=3 .
\]

Because \(3\) is prime, the product can be \(3\) only when **exactly one** prime
\(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) occurs in the factorisation of \(n\) and its exponent is \(\alpha=2\).
All other primes must be either \(2\) (with any exponent) or primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\) appearing with even exponents.

Consequently every admissible \(n\) can be written as  

\[
n = 2^{a}\,p^{2}\,t^{2},
\]

where  

* \(a\ge 0\) is an integer,  
* \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\) is a prime,  
* \(t\) is any integer whose prime factors are \(2\) or primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\) (the exponents of those primes are unrestricted because they appear squared).

Thus  

\[
n = 2^{a}\,m^{2}, \qquad m = p\;t .
\]

The integer \(m\) contains **exactly one** factor \(p\equiv 1\pmod4\) (to the first power); every other prime divisor of \(m\) is either \(2\) or \(\equiv3\pmod4\).

p = 5,\;13,\;17 .

p & \text{possible }m\;(m\le \sqrt{500/2^{a}}) \\ \hline

|0|5|\(25\)|

Higher powers of \(2\) ( \(a\ge2\) ) only reproduce numbers already obtained above, so no new \(n\) appear.

\boxed{25,\;50,\;100,\;169,\;200,\;289,\;338,\;400,\;450 } .

Each of these satisfies \(r_{2}(n)=12\); for example,
\(25=5^{2}\) gives the 12 points \((\pm5,0),\;(0,\pm5),\;(\pm3,\pm4),\;(\pm4,\pm3)\).

\[
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
\]

To count the lattice points that lie on a circle of radius \(\sqrt n\) centred at an integer lattice point \((a,b)\), we may translate the centre to the origin.  
Thus we need the number of integer solutions \((x,y)\) of  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=n .
\]

Every such solution \((x,y)\) gives a lattice point on the circle, and each solution with \((x,y)\neq (0,0)\) appears in eight symmetric positions  
\((\pm x,\pm y)\) and \((\pm y,\pm x)\) (unless \(x=0\) or \(y=0\) or \(|x|=|y|\), in which case the symmetry group is smaller).  
Hence the total number of lattice points on the circle is  

\[
r_{2}(n)=4\bigl(d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)\bigr),
\]

where \(d_{1}(n)\) (resp. \(d_{3}(n)\)) denotes the number of divisors of \(n\) that are \(\equiv 1\pmod 4\) (resp. \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\)).  
This classical formula follows from the factorisation of the Gaussian integer \(n\).

We want circles that pass through **exactly 12** lattice points, i.e. we need \(r_{2}(n)=12\).

\[
4\bigl(d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)\bigr)=12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)=3 .
\]

Thus we must find all \(n<500\) whose divisor‑difference \(d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)\) equals 3.

Recall that a positive integer \(n\) can be written uniquely as  

\[
n = 2^{e}\prod_{p\equiv1(4)}p^{\alpha_{p}}
          \prod_{q\equiv3(4)}q^{\beta_{q}},
\]

where the \(\alpha_{p},\beta_{q}\ge 0\).  
For such a factorisation the divisor‑difference is

\[
d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)=\prod_{p\equiv1(4)}(\alpha_{p}+1),
\]

because the primes \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\) contribute equally to \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{3}\) and therefore cancel.  
Consequently we need   

\[
\prod_{p\equiv1(4)}(\alpha_{p}+1)=3 .
\]

Since 3 is prime, the product can be 3 only in two ways:

1. One prime \(\equiv1\pmod4\) occurs to the first power (\(\alpha=2\)), all other such primes have exponent 0.
2. No prime \(\equiv1\pmod4\) occurs, which would give the product 1 – not admissible.

Thus **exactly one** prime congruent to 1 modulo 4 must appear in the factorisation of \(n\), and its exponent must be 2.  
All other prime factors of \(n\) may be any powers of the prime 2 or of primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\); they do not affect the value of \(r_{2}(n)\).

Hence every admissible \(n\) has the form  

\[
n = p^{2}\, m ,
\]

where \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) is a prime and \(m\) is any integer composed only of the prime 2 and of primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\).  

Now we enumerate all such numbers below 500.

| prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) | \(p^{2}\) | admissible multipliers \(m\) (≤ \(500/p^{2}\)) | resulting \(n\) |
|--------------------------|----------|--------------------------------|----------------|
| 5  | 25  | 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 13, 17, 20, 25 | 25, 50, 125, 200, 225, 325, 425, 500, 625 (≥500) |
| 13 | 169 | 1, 2, 3 | 169, 338, 507 (≥500) |
| 17 | 289 | 1, 2 | 289, 578 (≥500) |
| 29 | 841 (already >500) | – | – |
| 41 | 1681 (already >500) | – | – |

Collecting the values that are strictly less than 500 we obtain  

\[
25,\;50,\;169,\;200,\;225,\;289,\;338,\;400,\;450 .
\]

(Here the numbers 400 = \(20^{2}= (2^{2}\cdot5)^{2}\) and 450 = \(9\cdot5^{2}\) arise from choosing \(m=16\) and \(m=18\) respectively; both multipliers consist only of the allowed primes 2 and 3.)

Each of these nine integers indeed satisfies \(r_{2}(n)=12\), so for each there exists a circle centred at a lattice point with radius \(\sqrt{n}\) that passes through exactly twelve lattice points.

Finally, we add all admissible \(n\):

\[
25 + 50 + 169 + 200 + 225 + 289 + 338 + 400 + 450 = 2146 .
\]

Thus the required sum is  

\[
\boxed{2146}
\]

Let the centre of the circle be the lattice point \((a,b)\) and let its radius be \(\sqrt{n}\) with \(n\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\).
A lattice point \((x,y)\) lies on the circle exactly when  

\[
(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=n .
\]

Thus the number of lattice points on the circle is the number of integer solutions \((u,v)\) of  

\[
u^{2}+v^{2}=n ,\qquad u,v\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Hence the problem reduces to: **for which integers \(n<500\) does the Diophantine equation \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\) have exactly 12 integer solutions?**  
(Each solution \((u,v)\) corresponds to a lattice point on the circle, because we can translate back by the centre \((a,b)\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Number of representations of \(n\) as a sum of two squares  

Write the prime factorisation of \(n\) as  

\[
n=2^{\alpha}\prod_{p\equiv 1\,(4)}p^{\,\beta_{p}}\prod_{q\equiv 3\,(4)}q^{\,\gamma_{q}} .
\]

A classical theorem states that \(n\) is representable as a sum of two squares iff every prime
\(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) occurs with an even exponent \(\gamma_{q}\).  
When this condition holds, the number \(r_{2}(n)\) of **ordered** integer pairs \((u,v)\) (including signs and order) satisfying \(u^{2}+v^{2}=n\) is  

\[
r_{2}(n)=4\!\!\prod_{p\equiv 1\,(4)}(\beta_{p}+1).
\tag{1}
\]

(The factor \(4\) accounts for the four choices of signs, while the product counts the ways the
\(p\equiv1\pmod4\) prime powers can be distributed between the two squares.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  From ordered pairs to distinct lattice points  

Each unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) with \(u\neq0\neq v\) yields eight ordered solutions:
\((\pm u,\pm v)\) and \((\pm v,\pm u)\).  
If one of the coordinates is zero, we obtain only four ordered solutions.
If \(u=v=0\) we would have only one solution, but this cannot happen because \(n>0\).

Our requirement is **exactly 12 distinct lattice points** on the circle.  
Therefore we need exactly 12 ordered solutions, i.e.  

\[
r_{2}(n)=12 .
\tag{2}
\]

(If a solution with a zero coordinate occurred, we would have only \(4\) or \(8\) ordered
solutions, never \(12\); consequently all solutions must have both coordinates non‑zero, and the
count \(12\) already reflects the full set of ordered pairs.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Solving \(r_{2}(n)=12\)

From (1) we have  

\[
4\!\!\prod_{p\equiv 1\,(4)}(\beta_{p}+1)=12
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\prod_{p\equiv1\,(4)}(\beta_{p}+1)=3 .
\]

Hence the product of the factors \((\beta_{p}+1)\) must be \(3\).
Since each factor is a positive integer, the only possibility is that there is **exactly one**
prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) appearing in the factorisation, with exponent \(\beta_{p}=2\) (because
\(\beta_{p}+1=3\)). All other primes \( \equiv1\pmod4\) must be absent, and every prime
\(q\equiv3\pmod4\) must appear with an even exponent (including possibly \(0\)). The factor
\(2^{\alpha}\) is unrestricted.

Consequently every admissible \(n\) has the shape  

\[
n = 2^{\alpha}\,p^{2}\,\prod_{q\equiv 3\,(4)} q^{\,2\gamma_{q}},
\qquad p\equiv1\pmod4,\ \alpha,\gamma_{q}\ge 0 .
\tag{3}
\]

In words: \(n\) is a square multiple of a single prime \(p\equiv1\ (\text{mod }4)\), possibly
times any even powers of primes \(3\ (\text{mod }4)\) and any power of \(2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Searching \(n<500\)

We now list all numbers \(n<500\) of the form (3).

*Choose the prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\).*  
The smallest such primes are \(5,\,13,\,17,\,29,\,37,\,41,\,53,\dots\)

*Square the chosen prime:* \(p^{2}=25,\,169,\,289,\,841,\dots\)  
Only the squares not exceeding 500 are \(25,\,169,\,289\).

*Multiply by any power of 2 (including \(2^{0}=1\)), staying below 500.*  

| \(p^{2}\) | allowed powers of 2 | resulting numbers |
|-----------|--------------------|-------------------|
| \(25\)    | \(1,2,4,8,16\)     | \(25, 50, 100, 200, 400\) |
| \(169\)   | \(1,2\)            | \(169, 338\) |
| \(289\)   | \(1\)              | \(289\) |

*Now we may also multiply by any even power of a prime \(q\equiv3\pmod4\) (i.e. squares of 3,7,11,…).*
The smallest such square is \(3^{2}=9\).

Multiplying the numbers already listed by \(9\) would give  

\[
25\cdot9=225,\qquad 50\cdot9=450,\qquad 100\cdot9=900>500,
\]

and higher powers would exceed 500 as well.  
Thus the additional admissible values are \(225\) and \(450\).

Collecting all distinct numbers below 500 we obtain  

\[
25,\; 50,\; 100,\; 169,\; 200,\; 289,\; 338,\; 400,\; 450,\; 225 .
\]

### 5.  The required list  

The problem asks for the sum of **all** positive integers \(n<500\) satisfying the condition.
The complete set of such integers is  

\[

\]

These nine numbers are precisely those obtained from (3) that lie below 500.
